verses.text: How the gold has become dim! The most pure gold has changed! The stones of the sanctuary are poured out at the head of every street.
The precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, How are they esteemed as earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of the potter!
Even the jackals draw out the breast, they nurse their young ones: But the daughter of my people has become cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness.
The tongue of the nursing child clings to the roof of his mouth for thirst: The young children ask bread, and no man breaks it to them.
Those who fed delicately are desolate in the streets: Those who were brought up in scarlet embrace dunghills.
For the iniquity of the daughter of my people is greater than the sin of Sodom, That was overthrown as in a moment, and no hands were laid on her.
Her nobles were purer than snow, they were whiter than milk; They were more ruddy in body than rubies, their polishing was as of sapphire.
Their appearance is blacker than a coal; they are not known in the streets: Their skin clings to their bones; it is withered, it has become like a stick.
Those who are killed with the sword are better than those who are killed with hunger; For these pine away, stricken through, for want of the fruits of the field.
The hands of the pitiful women have boiled their own children; They were their food in the destruction of the daughter of my people.
Yahweh has accomplished his wrath, he has poured out his fierce anger; He has kindled a fire in Zion, which has devoured its foundations.
The kings of the earth didn’t believe, neither did all the inhabitants of the world, That the adversary and the enemy would enter into the gates of Jerusalem.
It is because of the sins of her prophets, and the iniquities of her priests, That have shed the blood of the just in the middle of her.
They wander as blind men in the streets. They are polluted with blood, So that men can’t touch their garments.
“Go away!” they cried to them, “Unclean! Go away! Go away! Don’t touch! When they fled away and wandered, men said among the nations, “They can’t live here any more.”
Yahweh’s anger has scattered them; he will no more regard them: They didn’t respect the persons of the priests, they didn’t favor the elders.
Our eyes still fail, looking in vain for our help: In our watching we have watched for a nation that could not save.
They hunt our steps, so that we can’t go in our streets: Our end is near, our days are fulfilled; for our end has come.
Our pursuers were swifter than the eagles of the sky: They chased us on the mountains, they laid wait for us in the wilderness.
The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of Yahweh, was taken in their pits; Of whom we said, Under his shadow we shall live among the nations.
Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Edom, that dwell in the land of Uz: The cup shall pass through to you also; you shall be drunken, and shall make yourself naked.
The punishment of your iniquity is accomplished, daughter of Zion; he will no more carry you away into captivity: He will visit your iniquity, daughter of Edom; he will uncover your sins.

footnotes.content: The poet sees gold grown dull—not just wealth lost, but the very brightness of God's dwelling made dark. When glory fades from a place we held sacred, it cuts deeper than any material loss. Yet he names it plainly, refusing to look away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those young ones, once precious beyond measure, now treated like common pottery—disposable. He grieves not for their lowness but for how swiftly a city forgets its children's worth. Jesus would know this sorrow well.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the wildest creatures tend their young; the poet draws the line starkly. Cruelty has become the new custom in Zion. Sometimes we must name our own failures aloud before healing can begin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A nursing child's tongue clinging to the roof of his mouth—that image stays with you. Hunger makes the strongest silent. When the smallest and most innocent suffer first, a city knows it has fallen into something dark.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those raised softly now sitting on ash heaps. The poet shows us no pity speech here, just the nakedness of reversed fortune. Humbling? Yes. And sometimes we need that stripping bare to remember what truly matters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sodom fell in fire, sudden and complete—but Jerusalem's sin seems somehow deeper, lingering in slow starvation. The poet names the comparison deliberately; he is not afraid of hard truth. God does not turn away from honest grief.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Snow, milk, rubies, sapphire—his eye remembers the nobles in their glory. Beauty and polish once marked their station. He honors the memory even as he prepares to name what becomes of them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Blacker than coal. Skin drawn tight to bone. They move through their own city unrecognized—a cruelty worse than exile. When famine rewrites the human face, we glimpse how close suffering can strip us to the bone, both body and spirit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Swift death seems kinder than the slow waste of hunger. The poet speaks what we dare not—that sometimes the sword is mercy. His honesty here is a door for the broken to name their own unbearable truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The most unspeakable horror: mothers, the guardians of life, reduced to starvation's darkest choice. He does not flinch from naming this. In doing so, he honors the depth of the city's fall and opens the way for God to answer in mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now he turns to speak of God's wrath—real, poured out, a fire that devoured Zion's foundations. This verse shifts the weight: judgment is not blind cruelty but the act of the Lord himself. That truth, though terrible, is also the ground of hope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the kings of the earth were astonished—they did not believe an enemy could breach Jerusalem's gates. But walls fail when God withdraws protection. The poet marks this as a turning point, a moment when the impossible became true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The prophets and priests—those who should have guarded the people—shed innocent blood in Jerusalem's heart. When the shepherds betray their trust, the flock suffers beyond measure. Yet even this betrayal does not surprise God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Blind men wandering, marked by blood so no one will touch them—the priesthood that once mediated holiness now wanders stained and untouchable. The poet captures the reversal: those who were set apart are now cast out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Unclean! Go away!" they cry to the exiles. Even among nations they are cast off, called unfit. He shows us the deepest shame: not just defeat in war, but rejection by the world itself, forbidden to dwell anywhere.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God's anger has scattered them; He looks on them no more. The very priests and elders—those who were to be honored—receive no regard from God's face. Yet it is this very abandonment that makes room for grace to return.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eyes failing, watching in vain for help that will not come. They looked to nations who could not save them. The poet names the futility plainly—and in naming it, he clears the air for a different kind of hope to grow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hunted even in their own streets, unable to walk freely. "Our end is near, our days are fulfilled." Death feels inevitable, final. Yet this moment of lowest darkness becomes the place where only God's resurrection can reach.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Swifter than eagles, hunted on mountains and in wilderness—there is no refuge left. The poet maps the totality of their pursuit. In this completeness of flight, he lets the reader feel the bottomless nature of defeat.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The anointed of the Lord, their king, was taken in the enemies' pits—captured like an animal. Once they trusted to live under his shadow among the nations; now he is prisoner. This verse marks the fall of Israel's earthly kingship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rejoice now, Edom—but the cup will pass to you too. Readers today hear an echo here: the nations that exult in another's fall do not see the reckoning turning toward them. The Lord's justice moves with a patience they cannot outrun.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Your punishment is accomplished, daughter of Zion—a word of terrible mercy. The sentence has been fulfilled, the wrath poured out. In this ending, a door opens: the possibility of being carried captive into restoration, not further ruin. Even judgment contains God's faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
